chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad ibn Isa, who said:

A man from the people of Basra came to Abu al-Hasan al-Awwal (peace be upon him) and said to him, 'May I be your ransom! I sit with a people who play with chess, and I do not play with it, but I just look.' He (peace be upon him) said, 'What is it to you and a gathering to which Allah does not look?'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on sitting and watching others play chess in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) clarifies that mere presence in the gathering of chess players incurs the same spiritual consequence as active participation, as indicated by the phrase 'a gathering to which Allah does not look.' This highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of *shubhat al-hukm* (similarity in ruling), where observers share in the status of the actors in a specific context. The Imam’s response underscores the importance of avoiding environments associated with leisure that may distract from spiritual mindfulness, even for non-players.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad Bin Isa who said,

‘A man from the (people of) Al-Basra came over to Abu Al-Hassan<sup>asws</sup> the 1st so he said to him<sup>asws</sup>, ‘May I be sacrificed for you<sup>asws</sup>! I sit with a people who are playing with the chess, and I do not play with it, but I (just) look’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘What is it to you and a gathering which Allah<sup>azwj</sup> does not Look at its people?’
en.sarwar: 12. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from Hammad ibn ‘Isa who has said the following:

“Once a man from the people of al-Basrah came to abu al-Hassan, al-Awwal, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, and said, ‘I pray to Allah to keep my soul in service for your cause, I sit with people who play chess but I do not play. I only look at it.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘What do you have to do with a gathering to which Allah does not look?”’
